p2.15.body:

p3.3.title: Problem 3.3 — Which goods fluctuate more than real GDP?
p3.3.body: [Chapter opener] Briefly explain whether production of each of the following is likely to fluctuate **more or less** than real GDP does during the business cycle.

questions.prompt: By roughly how many percent did real GDP per capita rise between 1961 and 2024?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (58,600 − 20,100) ÷ 20,100 × 100 = **191.5%**. Equivalently, real GDP per capita is about 2.9 times its 1961 level — 'almost three times as much' in the chapter's words.

questions.prompt: (b) Is the measured increase in real GDP per capita likely to be greater or less than the true increase in living standards?

options.text: Less than the true increase: real GDP per capita misses improvements in product quality and variety, health, leisure time and the environment
Greater than the true increase: real GDP per capita counts illegal and household production, so it overstates the gain
Exactly equal: real GDP per capita is a perfect measure of living standards once it is adjusted for inflation
Greater than the true increase: a larger population means nobody is better off even when real GDP per capita rises

questions.explanation: Real GDP per capita is the most common but **imperfect** measure of living standards. It does not capture better and entirely new products, longer life expectancy, more leisure or a cleaner environment. So the **measured increase is smaller than the true improvement** in living standards.

questions.prompt: (a) What does the rule of 70 say?

options.text: The growth rate of a variable equals 70 divided by the number of years it has been growing
The number of years it takes a variable to double is approximately 70 divided by its annual percentage growth rate
A variable doubles every 70 years regardless of its growth rate
A variable that grows at 70 percent per year doubles in one year

questions.explanation: The **rule of 70**: years to double ≈ 70 ÷ (annual growth rate in percent). The faster the growth, the sooner the doubling.

questions.prompt: (b) At 7 percent growth per year, about how many years will it take real GDP per capita to double?
What is the most important factor in explaining increases in real GDP per capita in the long run?

options.text: Increases in labour productivity
Increases in the size of the population
Increases in the price level
Increases in government purchases

questions.explanation: Long-run growth in real GDP per capita depends on **increases in labour productivity** (output per worker or per hour), which in turn depends on capital per hour worked and technology.

questions.prompt: What is potential real GDP, and does it stay constant over time?

options.text: It is the level of real GDP attained when all firms are producing at capacity; it stays constant because capacity is fixed
It is the highest level real GDP has ever reached; it is revised downward after each recession
It is the level of real GDP attained when all firms are producing at capacity; it grows over time as the labour force, capital and technology grow
It is the real GDP forecast for next year; it is unrelated to the capacity of firms

questions.explanation: **Potential GDP** is the level of real GDP when all firms produce at capacity. Because the labour force and capital stock grow and technology improves, it **rises over time**. (Your slides move the detail on potential GDP to Ch 8.)

source.note: Discussion question: most students would choose 2024; there is no single official answer.

questions.prompt: Would you rather live in Canada in 1900 on $1,000,000 or in Canada in 2024 on $50,000 (both in 2024 dollars)? Which statement best captures the economics?

options.text: Everyone should pick 1900, because the income is 20 times larger in real terms and real income is all that matters
It makes no difference, because real incomes in constant dollars are perfectly comparable across any two years
Everyone should pick 2024, because $50,000 is always worth more than $1,000,000 from a different year
Most people would pick 2024: $50,000 buys goods and services (modern medicine, electricity, communication, travel) that were unavailable in 1900 at any price

questions.explanation: Constant-dollar comparisons miss that many goods (antibiotics, refrigeration, the internet, air travel) were **not available at any price** in 1900, and life expectancy and quality of life were far lower. This is one reason real GDP per capita **understates** long-run improvements in living standards.

questions.prompt: [Apply the Concept: Economic Prosperity and Health] Higher incomes are associated with longer life expectancy. What does this imply for the health care sector in coming years?

options.text: It is likely to expand: richer, older populations spend a larger share of income on health care
It is likely to contract: longer life expectancy means people need less health care
It will stay the same share of the economy because health spending does not depend on income
It will contract because rising productivity reduces the demand for services

questions.explanation: As real incomes rise, households spend **more on health care**, and longer lives mean a larger elderly population that uses more care. The health care sector is therefore likely to **expand**.

questions.prompt: Based on this chapter, why does growth in real GDP per capita matter for the quality of life of a country's citizens?

options.text: It guarantees that income is distributed equally across the population
Sustained growth raises the typical person's purchasing power and pays for better health care, education and material comforts
It matters only because a larger real GDP lets a country pay off its debts
It is irrelevant to quality of life, because only the total size of the economy matters

questions.explanation: Rising real GDP per capita means **more goods and services per person**; the typical Canadian today can buy almost three times what the typical Canadian could in 1961. Growth makes better health, education and leisure affordable — though it does not guarantee equality.

questions.prompt: (a) What is the growth rate of real GDP in 1991? (percent)
(a) What is the growth rate of real GDP in 1992? (percent)
(a) What is the growth rate of real GDP in 1993? (percent)
(a) What is the growth rate of real GDP in 1994? (percent)
(b) What is the average annual growth rate of real GDP over 1991–1994? (percent)
questions.explanation: Average the four annual growth rates, as on the slides: (-0.24 + 3.39 + 2.85 + 4.08) ÷ 4 = **2.52%**.

questions.prompt: If Canada keeps growing at 1.6 percent per year, approximately how many years until real GDP per capita doubles?
questions.explanation: Rule of 70: 70 ÷ 1.6 = 43.75, i.e. about **44 years**.

questions.prompt: If productivity gains lift growth to 2 percent per year, how many years until real GDP per capita doubles?
questions.explanation: 70 ÷ 2 = **35 years**, roughly 9 years sooner. Small differences in growth rates compound into big differences in living standards.

source.note: Discussion question with no single official answer.

questions.prompt: [Solved Problem 6.1] The steps needed to improve Canada's slow growth sound simple (more investment, more innovation). What might prevent the government from taking them?

options.text: Economic theory shows that investment and innovation cannot raise labour productivity
Governments cannot change tax or spending policy in Canada
Growth-promoting policies often impose costs now for benefits later, and they create losers who lobby against them, so political constraints can block them
Faster growth would cause real GDP per capita to fall in the long run

questions.explanation: Growth-friendly reforms (investment incentives, deregulation, education, openness) have **up-front costs and delayed benefits** and face opposition from groups that lose, so **political and trade-off obstacles** often matter more than the economics.

questions.prompt: (a) If Smith's estimates are correct, is the growth rate of labour productivity measured by government statistics overstated or understated?

options.text: Overstated: official hours are too low, so measured output per hour is too high
Overstated: slacking raises output, which is counted twice in GDP
Neither: labour productivity is calculated from output alone, so hours worked are irrelevant
Understated: output is divided by official hours, which exceed hours actually worked, so true output per hour worked is higher than measured

questions.explanation: Labour productivity = real GDP ÷ **hours worked**. If actual hours are only 85.5% of official hours, dividing by the larger official figure gives a number that is **too low**: measured productivity (and its growth, if slacking has increased) is understated.

questions.prompt: (b) What does this imply for using official real GDP per capita to measure increases in well-being?

options.text: Official real GDP per capita probably understates the gain in well-being, since workers also enjoy leisure-like time that GDP does not count
It overstates the gain in well-being, because slacking reduces total output
It has no implications, because GDP per capita measures only well-being from work
It means GDP per capita should be replaced by hours worked as the only measure of well-being

questions.explanation: Official statistics count the time as work, so they miss the extra non-market benefit (leisure) that workers enjoy. Like quality improvements and unpaid work, this is another way that **real GDP per capita understates** gains in well-being.

questions.prompt: Why should we expect a close relationship between productivity gains and increases in real wages?

options.text: Higher productivity lets firms pay lower wages because workers can work fewer hours
Firms pay workers roughly the value of what they produce, so when output per hour rises across the economy, competition for workers pushes real wages up
Real wages are set by the government in line with productivity statistics
Productivity gains raise prices by exactly the amount of wages, leaving real wages unchanged

questions.explanation: A worker's pay is tied to the **value of the output the worker produces**. When productivity rises economy-wide, firms compete for workers and real wages rise. In Britain (1770–1830) gains were confined to a few industries, so real wages barely moved until gains spread across the economy.

questions.prompt: Why is the financial system important for long-run growth, and why must firms have access to adequate funds?

options.text: Firms never need outside funds because retained earnings always cover investment; the financial system matters only for households
Growth depends only on government borrowing; the private financial system has no role
Firms need funds to buy capital and adopt new technology; the financial system channels household saving to them, so a well-functioning system supports investment and growth
The financial system creates funds out of nothing, so saving is not needed for investment

questions.explanation: Growth requires more capital per hour worked and new technology. Many firms cannot finance rapid expansion from retained earnings, so they rely on **households' saving channelled through financial markets and intermediaries**.

questions.prompt: Why must total saving equal total investment in a closed economy?

options.text: Because the government forces households to save exactly as much as firms want to invest
Because investment is defined as the saving done by households, ignoring government
Because interest rates are set by the central bank so that the two always match
Y = C + I + G, so I = Y − C − G; and national saving (private plus public) also equals Y − C − G, hence S = I

questions.explanation: In a closed economy Y = C + I + G → **I = Y − C − G**. Private saving (Y + TR − C − T) plus public saving (T − G − TR) also simplifies to **Y − C − G**, so **S = I** by accounting. The loanable funds market is how that equality is reached.

questions.prompt: What are loanable funds, and who demands and supplies them?

options.text: Funds available to be borrowed; businesses demand them to finance investment projects and households (plus government surpluses) supply them as saving
Funds held by the central bank; the government demands them and firms supply them
Funds from foreign countries only; domestic households play no role
Funds firms raise only through the stock market; households demand them to buy cars

questions.explanation: **Loanable funds** are the funds savers make available to borrowers. **Firms demand** them to finance new investment projects (more projects are profitable at low rates); **households supply** them through saving, and government budget surpluses add to supply.

questions.prompt: You can earn 3 percent on a bank CD while the bank charges 7 percent on car loans. Why might you refuse to lend directly to a borrower who offers more than 3 percent?

options.text: Lending directly is illegal in Canada
You would bear that borrower's default risk and information costs and lose liquidity; the bank diversifies risk, screens borrowers and lets you get your money back
Interest paid by an individual borrower is always taxed at 100 percent
Individual borrowers never repay loans, whereas banks never lose money

questions.explanation: Intermediaries provide the three key services: **risk-sharing** (your deposit is backed by many loans), **information** (the bank screens and monitors borrowers) and **liquidity** (you can withdraw). Lending to one person exposes you to default risk and information costs, with no easy exit.

questions.prompt: (a) Private saving ($ trillion)?
questions.explanation: S<sub>private</sub> = Y + TR − C − T = 11 + 1 − 8 − 3 = **$1 trillion**.

questions.prompt: (b) Public saving ($ trillion)? (Hint: total saving S equals I.)
questions.explanation: Total saving equals investment: S = I = 2. So S<sub>public</sub> = S − S<sub>private</sub> = 2 − 1 = **$1 trillion** (check: T − G − TR = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1).

questions.prompt: (c) Government purchases ($ trillion)? (In a closed economy Y = C + I + G.)
questions.explanation: G = Y − C − I = 11 − 8 − 2 = **$1 trillion**.

questions.prompt: (d) What is the government's budget position?

options.text: A budget surplus of $1 trillion (public saving is positive)
A budget deficit of $1 trillion
A balanced budget
A budget deficit of $2 trillion

questions.explanation: The budget balance equals public saving: T − G − TR = **+$1 trillion**, a **surplus** (taxes of $3 trillion exceed G + TR = $2 trillion).

questions.prompt: (a) Private saving ($ trillion)? (Hint: first find total saving S = Y − C − G.)
questions.explanation: S = Y − C − G = 12 − 8 − 2 = 2, and S = S<sub>private</sub> + S<sub>public</sub>, so S<sub>private</sub> = 2 − (−0.5) = **$2.5 trillion**.

questions.prompt: (b) Investment spending ($ trillion)?
questions.explanation: In a closed economy S = I. Total saving is 2.5 + (−0.5) = 2, so **I = $2 trillion** (also I = Y − C − G = 12 − 8 − 2).

questions.prompt: (c) Transfer payments TR ($ trillion)?
questions.explanation: S<sub>public</sub> = T − G − TR → −0.5 = 2 − 2 − TR → TR = **$0.5 trillion**. (Check: S<sub>private</sub> = 12 + 0.5 − 8 − 2 = 2.5.)

questions.prompt: (d) What is the government's budget position?

options.text: A budget surplus of $0.5 trillion
A budget deficit of $0.5 trillion
A balanced budget
A budget deficit of $2 trillion

questions.explanation: Public saving is −$0.5 trillion: T = 2 is less than G + TR = 2.5, so the government runs a **deficit of $0.5 trillion**.

questions.prompt: (a) What is total saving S now ($ trillion)?
questions.explanation: S = Y − C − G = 12 − 8 − 2.5 = **$1.5 trillion**. Private saving is unchanged at 2.5; public saving falls from −0.5 to −1.0.

questions.prompt: (b) What is investment I now ($ trillion)?
questions.explanation: Since S = I, investment falls from 2.0 to **$1.5 trillion**.

questions.prompt: (c) What does this illustrate?

options.text: Crowding in: higher government purchases raise private investment by the same amount
Nothing changes, because saving and investment are determined independently
Crowding out: with Y and C fixed, extra government purchases lower national saving and therefore investment one for one
Investment rises by $0.5 trillion, because the government spends the funds on capital

questions.explanation: With Y and C fixed, Y − C − G falls by the $0.5 trillion rise in G, so S and I each fall by $0.5 trillion: government purchases **crowd out** private investment.

questions.prompt: (a) The shift from S₁ to S₂ is…

options.text: An increase in the supply of loanable funds
A decrease in the quantity supplied (a movement along S₁)
An increase in the demand for loanable funds
A decrease in the supply of loanable funds

questions.explanation: S₂ lies to the **left** of S₁: less is supplied at every interest rate, so supply has **decreased** (a shift, not a movement along the curve).

questions.prompt: (b) What happens to the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds and the real interest rate?

options.text: The quantity falls (L₂ < L₁) and the real interest rate rises (i₂ > i₁)
The quantity rises and the real interest rate falls
The quantity falls and the real interest rate falls
The quantity is unchanged and only the real interest rate rises

questions.explanation: A leftward supply shift against an unchanged downward-sloping demand curve **raises the real interest rate and lowers the equilibrium quantity**.

questions.prompt: (c) What happens to the quantity of saving and the quantity of investment?

options.text: Saving falls but investment rises
Both fall, by the same amount
Saving rises but investment falls
Both rise, by the same amount

questions.explanation: The equilibrium quantity of loanable funds is both the amount saved and the amount invested (S = I). With L falling from L₁ to L₂, **saving and investment both fall**.

questions.prompt: (a) After the demand shift (A to C), what happens to the equilibrium real interest rate and quantity of loanable funds?

options.text: The interest rate rises and the quantity falls
The interest rate falls and the quantity rises
Both rise
Both fall

questions.explanation: Demand increased, so the equilibrium moves up along the unchanged supply curve: a **higher real interest rate (i₂ > i₁) and more loanable funds (L₂ > L₁)**.

questions.prompt: (b) How can the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds increase when the interest rate rises? Doesn't a higher rate reduce the quantity demanded?

options.text: The law of demand does not hold for loanable funds, so a higher interest rate raises the quantity demanded
The supply curve also shifted right, which raised the quantity
The quantity of loanable funds increases only because the interest rate is set by the government

The demand curve itself shifted right; a higher rate reduces the quantity demanded only along a given curve, and the rate rises just enough to cut the quantity demanded from L₃ back to L₂ while raising the quantity supplied

questions.explanation: A higher rate lowers the quantity demanded only **along a given demand curve**. Here demand shifted right, so at every rate firms want more. The rate rises until the quantity supplied (a movement **along S₁**) equals the quantity demanded on D₂: below L₃ (point B) but above L₁ (point A).

questions.prompt: (a) What is the likely effect of the expansion on the expected profitability of new investment in plant and equipment?

options.text: It rises: higher expected sales and capacity use make new projects more profitable
It falls: firms already have excess capacity
It is unaffected: profitability depends only on the interest rate
It rises, but only for firms that already own plants

questions.explanation: In an expansion demand for goods and services grows, so firms expect **higher sales and profits** from new plant and equipment.

questions.prompt: (b) In the loanable funds market, which curve shifts, and in which direction?

options.text: The supply curve shifts right
The demand curve shifts right (firms want to borrow more at every interest rate)
The demand curve shifts left
The supply curve shifts left

questions.explanation: Higher expected profitability raises the demand for loanable funds: **D shifts right**. Supply is held unchanged, as in the lecture's treatment.

questions.prompt: Show the effect of the forecast on the market for loanable funds. Draw the new demand curve D₂ and mark the new equilibrium E₂.

tasks.label: D₂
tasks.prompt: Draw the new demand curve D₂

questions.explanation: A forecast of expansion raises the **expected profitability of new investment**, so firms want to borrow more at every real interest rate: **demand for loanable funds shifts right**. Supply is unchanged, so the equilibrium real interest rate **and** the quantity of loanable funds both rise (a movement up along S).

questions.prompt: (c) What happens to the equilibrium real interest rate, the quantity of loanable funds, saving and investment?

options.text: The real interest rate falls; saving and investment rise
The real interest rate rises; saving and investment fall
The real interest rate rises; the quantity of loanable funds, saving and investment all rise
The real interest rate is unchanged; investment rises while saving is unchanged

questions.explanation: A right shift in demand raises the equilibrium **real interest rate** and moves along the supply curve to a larger quantity: saving (the quantity supplied) rises and so does investment, since S = I.

questions.prompt: (a) Which curve shifts in the loanable funds market?

options.text: Demand shifts right, because firms need to borrow to pay the tax
Supply shifts right, because the government has more revenue to lend
Supply shifts left, because households save less
Demand shifts left, because the after-tax return on investment projects falls

questions.explanation: A higher profit tax reduces the **after-tax return** on projects, so fewer projects are worth financing at each interest rate: **D shifts left**. With the budget balance held fixed, supply is unchanged.

questions.prompt: (b) What happens to the equilibrium real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds?

options.text: Both fall
Both rise
The interest rate falls and the quantity rises
The interest rate rises and the quantity falls

questions.explanation: A left shift in demand along an unchanged supply curve gives a **lower real interest rate and a smaller quantity** of loanable funds.

questions.prompt: (c) What is the effect on investment by firms and on the economy's future capital stock?

options.text: Investment rises, so the capital stock will be larger
Investment falls, so the capital stock will be smaller (and growth slower) than otherwise
Investment is unchanged, so the capital stock is unchanged
Investment falls, but the capital stock rises because the interest rate is lower

questions.explanation: A lower L means **less investment** and so less capital accumulation. A smaller capital stock per hour worked means lower future labour productivity and slower growth.

questions.prompt: (a) What is the effect of shrinking budget deficits on the market for loanable funds?

options.text: Supply shifts left: the real interest rate rises and investment falls
Demand shifts left: the real interest rate falls and investment falls
Public saving rises, so supply shifts right: the real interest rate falls and saving, investment and loanable funds all rise
Demand shifts right: the real interest rate rises and investment rises

questions.explanation: A smaller deficit means higher **public saving** and so higher national saving: **S shifts right**, lowering the real interest rate and raising the quantity of loanable funds. Saving and investment both increase (less crowding out).

questions.prompt: (b) Households expect lower taxes soon and cut their saving. How does this change the analysis in (a)?

options.text: The supply shift is larger, because lower taxes make deficit cuts more effective
Demand shifts right, so the interest rate rises and completely reverses part (a)
Nothing changes, because private saving never responds to expected taxes
Private saving falls and partly offsets the rise in public saving, so supply shifts right by less: the interest rate falls less and the quantity rises less

questions.explanation: Lower household saving shifts S back to the left, **partially offsetting** the increase from public saving. The net rightward shift of S is smaller, so the fall in the interest rate and the rise in investment are **smaller** than with deficit cuts alone.

questions.prompt: (a) What happens to savers' after-tax return, and which curve shifts?

options.text: After-tax real return rises, so households save more at each interest rate and supply shifts right
After-tax real return falls, so supply shifts left
Firms' after-tax profits rise, so demand shifts right
Nothing changes because the tax is paid by borrowers

questions.explanation: Taxing nominal interest taxes the inflation component too, which can leave a low or negative after-tax real return. Taxing only real interest **raises the after-tax real return** to saving, so **S shifts right**.

questions.prompt: (b) What happens to the equilibrium real interest rate, saving and investment?

options.text: The real interest rate rises; saving and investment rise
The real interest rate falls; the quantity of loanable funds, saving and investment all rise
The real interest rate falls; saving and investment fall
The real interest rate rises; saving rises but investment falls

questions.explanation: A right shift in supply along an unchanged demand curve → **lower real interest rate, larger quantity**. Saving and investment each rise (S = I).

questions.prompt: The IMF says a country's financial system provides a framework supporting economic growth. Do you agree?

options.text: No: growth depends only on natural resources; finance is irrelevant
No: financial systems always reduce saving and investment
Yes: a sound financial system channels saving to productive investments and provides risk-sharing, liquidity and information, which supports capital accumulation and growth
Yes, but only because a sound financial system guarantees that no recession will ever occur

questions.explanation: A well-functioning financial system links savers and borrowers and provides **risk-sharing, liquidity and information**, so more funds reach productive uses and investment and growth rise. It does not abolish recessions.

questions.prompt: (b) How does AI affect labour productivity in the financial system?

options.text: It raises it: the same output of financial services is produced with fewer hours of labour
It lowers it: workers become less skilled
It has no effect because services cannot be measured
It lowers it because technology replaces capital

questions.explanation: Labour productivity is output per hour worked. If AI lets firms deliver the same services with less human labour, **output per hour rises**.

source.note: Ambiguous: AI could instead raise the profitability of investment (demand right). Either way investment rises; the supply-side reading was chosen.

questions.prompt: (c) Using the loanable funds model, how would AI-driven cost reductions affect long-run growth?

options.text: Lower costs shift demand left, lowering investment and growth
Cheaper intermediation raises the supply of loanable funds, lowering the real interest rate and raising investment, capital and long-run growth
Lower costs raise the real interest rate and reduce saving
There is no effect because the loanable funds market is unaffected by costs

questions.explanation: Lower costs raise the **net return to savers** and make saving through the financial system more attractive: **S shifts right**, the real interest rate falls and investment rises. More capital per hour worked boosts productivity and growth.

questions.prompt: (a) What typically happens to inflation over the cycle?

options.text: It rises during recessions and falls during expansions
It is unaffected by the business cycle
It tends to rise toward the end of an expansion and fall during a recession
It is highest at the trough

questions.explanation: In an expansion demand is high relative to supply, so prices rise faster (especially late in the expansion); in a recession demand is weak, so inflation falls (prices may even fall).

questions.prompt: (b) What typically happens to the unemployment rate over the cycle?

options.text: It rises throughout an expansion
It stays constant at the natural rate
It rises during an expansion and falls during a recession
It declines during the later part of an expansion and rises during a recession

questions.explanation: Unemployment moves **opposite to output**: it falls as production and hiring expand, and rises in recession.

questions.prompt: (c) Why might the unemployment rate keep rising in the early stages of an expansion?

options.text: Firms may be slow to rehire, and discouraged workers re-enter the labour force as conditions improve, so unemployment can rise even as output recovers
Because output falls at the start of every expansion
Because inflation falls too fast for firms to hire
Because every expansion begins with a new recession

questions.explanation: Early in a recovery firms first raise hours of existing workers and are cautious about hiring; meanwhile **discouraged workers** start looking again, adding to the labour force and the unemployed. So unemployment often keeps rising after the trough.

questions.prompt: No agency in Canada is responsible for declaring recessions. Why might Statistics Canada not want that role?

options.text: Statistics Canada does not collect any data on GDP or employment
Declaring recessions is judgmental and politically sensitive, and its own GDP data get revised, so a declaration could later look wrong and damage its credibility
The Canadian constitution forbids federal agencies from measuring GDP
Recessions are defined only by the Bank of Canada, whose decisions cannot be questioned

questions.explanation: Dating a recession involves **judgment** across duration, depth and breadth, and the underlying data are **revised** (see the Week 6 lecture). A neutral statistical agency would not want to be accused of political bias or to reverse itself, so dating is left to non-official bodies like the C.D. Howe Business Cycle Council.

questions.prompt: Some firms prosper by expanding during recessions. What risks does the strategy carry?

options.text: There is no risk because recessions always end within two quarters
Expanding in a recession is illegal under competition law
The recession may be deeper or longer than expected, leaving the firm with debt and idle capacity; caution is warranted in highly cyclical industries or when the firm is heavily indebted
The only risk is that interest rates will fall

questions.explanation: Expanding during a recession can capture cheap inputs and market share, but if the downturn **lasts longer or goes deeper** than forecast, sales fall short of the new capacity and debt payments strain finances. Firms whose demand is very cyclical (e.g. autos, aircraft) or already highly leveraged should be more cautious.

questions.prompt: 'Real GDP in 2012 was $1.6 trillion. This value is a large number. Therefore, economic growth must have been high during 2012.' Do you agree?

options.text: Yes: a large level of real GDP always means rapid growth
Yes: growth is defined as the level of real GDP divided by population
No: real GDP of $1.6 trillion is too small for a large economy
No: the level of real GDP says nothing about growth, which is the percentage change in real GDP from the previous year

questions.explanation: Economic growth is measured by the **percentage change** in real GDP, not its level. A large economy can be growing slowly, or even shrinking.

questions.prompt: Samuelson argued the Great Moderation caused the Great Recession. Why might it have made the severe 2007–2009 recession more likely?

options.text: Years of stable growth led borrowers and lenders to underestimate risk and take on heavy debt, so when the downturn came, defaults and losses were severe
Stable growth reduced consumers' incomes, forcing them to default
Stable growth caused lenders to restrict credit, starving firms of funds
It could not have: stability of output always makes recessions milder

questions.explanation: During the Great Moderation recessions were mild and rare, so consumers felt secure borrowing and lenders felt safe lending more freely. The result was **high leverage**; when the housing and financial shocks hit, defaults cascaded and the downturn was deep.
